title: Properties of solids, liquids and gases
competency: Describe the arrangement, spacing and motion of particles in solids, liquids and gases.

keywords.def: Matter with a definite shape and volume. Its particles are packed tightly and only vibrate.
Matter with a definite volume but no definite shape. Its particles slide past each other.
Matter with no definite shape or volume. Its particles are far apart and move freely.
A substance that can flow. Liquids and gases are fluids.
Can be squeezed into a smaller volume.

en.text: In solids the particles are packed tightly in a fixed pattern and only vibrate. In liquids the particles are close but can slide past each other. In gases the particles are far apart and move freely. A gas is mostly empty space.

screens.title: Pour it
screens.ask: Which one can you pour into a cup?
screens.after: Water is a liquid. Its particles can slide past each other, so it flows.

screens.title: 2.1.5 Properties of solids, liquids and gases
paras: By the particle theory, all matter is made of tiny particles.
The particles are arranged differently in solids, liquids and gases.

screens.title: Figures 2.1–2.3: how the particles sit
items: Particles in a fixed pattern, tightly packed. They vibrate but stay in place. Stones, wood, metals.
Particles close, with spaces to slide past each other. Takes the shape of its container. Water, oil, ethanol.
Particles very far apart. Mostly empty space. Air, oxygen, carbon dioxide, nitrogen.

screens.title: Key words
defs: Matter with a definite shape and volume. Its particles are packed tightly and only vibrate.
Matter with a definite volume but no definite shape. Its particles slide past each other.
Matter with no definite shape or volume. Its particles are far apart and move freely.

screens.text: Particles in solids: in which state do particles only vibrate in a fixed place?
screens.why:
Solid particles are packed tightly in a fixed pattern.
Strong forces hold each one in place.
They can only vibrate (shake) where they are.
Liquid particles slide; gas particles move freely.
Answer: solid.
screens.clue: Which state keeps its own shape?

screens.title: Sort by state at room temperature
screens.why:
Does it keep its own shape? Then it is a solid: stone, wood.
Does it flow but keep its volume? Then it is a liquid: cooking oil, ethanol.
Does it spread out to fill the container? Then it is a gas: oxygen, carbon dioxide.
screens.clue: Does it keep its shape? Does it fill the whole container?
screens.text: Sort each substance by its state at room temperature.
Particle arrangement: in which state are particles very close together in a regular pattern?
screens.why:
Solid: particles very close, in a regular (orderly) pattern.
Liquid: close, but less orderly.
Gas: very far apart and disorderly.
Only the solid is both very close and regular.
Answer: solid.

screens.text: Particles in gases and liquids: why can a gas fill a whole room but a liquid stays at the bottom of a cup?
opts: Gas particles are far apart and move freely in all directions
screens.ans: Gas particles are far apart and move freely in all directions
screens.why:
Gas particles are very far apart, with almost no attraction between them.
They move freely in all directions, so they spread to fill the room.
Liquid particles stay close together, held by stronger forces.
So the liquid stays at the bottom of the cup.
"Gas particles are heavier" is wrong: gases have the lowest density.

en.text: Solids have a definite shape and volume. They cannot be poured or squeezed. Liquids have a definite volume but take the shape of the container. Gases have no definite shape or volume and fill the container. Liquids and gases flow, so they are fluids. Gases are easily compressed.

screens.title: Squeeze the air
screens.ask: You push the plunger of a syringe full of air with your finger over the end. What happens?
opts: It moves in: air can be squeezed
screens.after: Air is a gas. Its particles are far apart, so it can be squeezed into less space.
screens.best: It moves in: air can be squeezed

screens.title: Table 2.1 Properties of solids, liquids and gases
What the three states share
sets: Definite shape and volume. Not compressible. Particles vibrate in a fixed place.
Definite volume, no definite shape. Only very slightly compressible.
No definite shape or volume. Highly compressible. Fills its container.
overlaps: Solids and liquids both keep their volume.
Liquids and gases both flow and take the shape of their container.
All are matter, made of tiny moving particles.

screens.title: Key words
defs: A substance that can flow. Liquids and gases are fluids.
Can be squeezed into a smaller volume.

screens.text: Compressibility: which state of matter can be compressed easily?
screens.why:
To compress means to squeeze into a smaller volume.
Gas particles are very far apart: a gas is mostly empty space.
Pushing moves the particles closer into that space.
Solid and liquid particles are already close.
Answer: gas.

screens.text: Fluids: which states of matter are fluids?
screens.why:
A fluid is a substance that can flow.
Liquids flow: water pours.
Gases flow too: moving air is wind.
Solids keep their shape and do not flow.
Answer: liquid and gas.

pairs: Definite volume, takes the shape of the container
No definite shape or volume, fills the container
screens.why:
Solid: particles fixed in place, so definite shape and definite volume.
Liquid: particles slide but stay close, so definite volume but the shape of the container.
Gas: particles far apart and free, so no definite shape or volume; it fills the container.
screens.clue: Which one keeps its own shape?
screens.text: Match each state to its shape and volume.
True or false: liquids and solids both have a definite volume.
screens.why:
A solid keeps its own volume.
1 litre of water poured into another bottle is still 1 litre.
So a liquid keeps its volume too; only its shape changes.
The statement is true.
screens.clue: Does 1 litre of water stay 1 litre in a new bottle?

screens.text: Shape and volume of a liquid: a 1-litre bottle of water is poured into a 2-litre jug. What is true?
opts: The water now has a volume of 2 litres
The water keeps 1 litre but takes the jug's shape
The water keeps the bottle's shape
screens.ans: The water keeps 1 litre but takes the jug's shape
screens.why:
A liquid has a definite volume: the water stays 1 litre.
A liquid has no definite shape: it takes the shape of the jug.
It does not spread to fill 2 litres; only a gas would.
Answer: the water keeps 1 litre but takes the jug's shape.
screens.clue: Which properties does a liquid keep?

items.text: Exercise 2.4: what are the three states of matter?
items.why:
Matter exists in three states.
Ice, water and steam are one example: solid, liquid and gas.
"Ice, water and steam only" is too narrow: those are the states of one substance.
Answer: solid, liquid and gas.
items.clue: Think of ice, water and steam.

items.text: Exercise 2.4: which is a property of solids?
opts: They have a definite shape and volume
items.ans: They have a definite shape and volume
items.why:
Solid particles are fixed in place.
So a solid keeps its own shape and its own volume.
It does not flow and is not easily compressed.
Answer: they have a definite shape and volume.
items.clue: Does a stone change shape in a cup?

items.text: Exercise 2.4: name a property of liquids that solids do not share.
opts: Liquids can flow and take the shape of their container
items.ans: Liquids can flow and take the shape of their container
items.why:
Liquid particles slide past each other.
So a liquid flows and takes the shape of its container.
Solid particles are fixed, so a solid keeps its shape.
Volume, mass and particles are shared by both, so those options are wrong.
items.clue: What can water do that a stone cannot?

items.text: Exercise 2.4: name a property of gases that liquids do not share.
opts: Gases have no definite volume and fill the container
items.ans: Gases have no definite volume and fill the container
items.why:
Liquids and gases can both flow.
A liquid keeps its volume; a gas does not.
Gas particles spread out to fill any container.
Answer: gases have no definite volume and fill the container.

items.text: Exercise 2.4: give a characteristic that is the same for gases and liquids.
items.why:
Liquids and gases are both fluids.
That means both can flow, and neither has a definite shape.
Only a liquid has a definite volume; only a gas is easily compressed.
Answer: both can flow.

items.text: Exercise 2.4: which state of matter cannot be poured?
items.why:
Pouring needs a substance that flows.
Liquids and gases are fluids: they flow.
Solid particles are fixed in place, so a solid keeps its shape.
Answer: solid.
items.clue: Which one keeps its own shape?

items.text: Exercise 2.4: which state of matter is fluid? (A solid, B liquid, C gas)
items.why:
A fluid can flow.
Liquid (B) flows and gas (C) flows.
Solid (A) keeps its shape.
So the answer is B and C: liquid and gas.

items.text: Exercise 2.4: in which state of matter are particles close together?
items.why:
Solid particles are very close, in a regular pattern.
Liquid particles are also fairly close, but less orderly.
Gas particles are far apart.
The book's answer is solid: its particles are the closest.

test.text: Shape and volume: which state has a definite shape and a definite volume?
test.why:
Solid particles are fixed in place.
So a solid keeps its shape and its volume.
A liquid keeps only its volume; a gas keeps neither.
Answer: solid.

test.text: True or false: a gas has neither a definite volume nor a definite shape.
test.why:
Gas particles are far apart and move freely.
They spread out to fill any container.
So a gas takes the shape and volume of its container.
The statement is true.

test.text: Compressibility: why are gases easy to compress?
test.why:
A gas is mostly empty space.
Its particles are far apart.
Squeezing pushes them closer together.
Answer: their particles are far apart.

test.text: Fluids: which two states are fluids?
test.why:
A fluid is a substance that can flow.
Liquids pour and gases spread: both flow.
Solids keep their shape.
Answer: liquid and gas.

test.text: Solid → liquid → gas: which of these decreases?
test.why:
Distance between particles increases: close → far.
Speed and energy of the particles increase.
Order goes orderly → less orderly → disorderly.
So order among particles is the one that decreases.

notes.text: Table 2.1 says solids are "denser than all". Ice floats on water, so the lesson says "usually highest". Teacher to confirm.
